title: Febrile seizures
subject: paediatrics
summary: A seizure with fever of 38 °C or more in a child aged 6 to 60 months without CNS infection. After a simple febrile seizure, look for the cause of fever; do LP only if meningitis is suspected (an option if Hib or pneumococcal immunisation is incomplete or after antibiotics); no routine EEG, imaging or preventive antiepileptics.

sections.title: Definitions
items: Febrile seizure: seizure with fever of 38 °C or more in a child aged 6 to 60 months (some guidelines 6 months to 6 years) without CNS infection, metabolic disturbance or previous afebrile seizures.
Simple: generalised, lasting under 15 minutes, not recurring within 24 hours or the same illness, with full recovery within 1 hour.
Complex: focal features, lasting 15 minutes or more, recurring within 24 hours or the same illness, or altered consciousness for over 1 hour. Febrile status epilepticus: 30 minutes or more.
Red flags for CNS infection: meningism, bulging fontanelle, petechial rash, drowsiness persisting beyond 1 hour, focal deficit, recent antibiotics, or incomplete Hib or pneumococcal immunisation.

sections.title: If the child is still seizing
items: Airway, oxygen, recovery position, check blood glucose, and time the seizure.

If the seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, give a benzodiazepine: buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg), or IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg), or IV diazepam 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg), or rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg (max 10 mg). A second dose may be given once after 5 to 10 minutes.

Still seizing after two benzodiazepine doses: manage as convulsive status epilepticus with a second-line agent (levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate) per the status epilepticus protocol and involve a senior.

sections.title: Evaluation (AAP 2011)
items: Focus on finding the cause of fever (examination, urine test in infants, targeted tests). A simple febrile seizure carries the same risk of serious bacterial infection as fever alone.

Lumbar puncture: do it if there are signs or symptoms of meningitis or intracranial infection. It is an option at 6 to 12 months if Hib or pneumococcal immunisation is deficient or unknown, and in children pretreated with antibiotics, which can mask meningitis.
After a simple febrile seizure do not routinely order EEG, blood tests (electrolytes, calcium) or neuroimaging; check glucose if the child is drowsy.
Complex seizure: targeted tests (glucose, electrolytes), lower threshold for LP, and discuss neuroimaging and EEG with a senior, especially with focal features or delayed recovery.

sections.title: After the seizure
items: Treat the cause of the fever. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4 to 6 hours (max 60 mg/kg/day) may be given for comfort, but antipyretics do not prevent recurrence.
Do not start continuous or intermittent antiepileptic prophylaxis after simple febrile seizures (AAP 2008): the risks outweigh the small benefit.
After a prolonged febrile seizure (5 minutes or more), consider a home rescue plan with buccal midazolam and train the carers.

sections.title: Admit, refer or discharge
items: Discharge after a simple febrile seizure when the child is back to neurological baseline and the fever source is assessed, with seizure first-aid education and a written handout.

Discuss with or admit under paediatrics: complex seizure, suspected meningitis or sepsis, not back to baseline within 1 hour, or carers unable to cope or far from care. Transfer if prolonged seizure or respiratory or circulatory compromise.

Outpatient paediatric follow-up: prolonged or recurrent complex seizures, developmental concerns, neurocutaneous stigmata, family history of epilepsy, or febrile seizures after 6 years; EEG, imaging or genetic tests may then be considered.

sections.title: Counselling parents
items: Febrile seizures affect 2 to 5% of children aged 6 to 60 months and do not cause brain damage. After simple febrile seizures, the risk of epilepsy is about 1%, similar to the general population.
Recurrence is common, especially when the first seizure is early: about 50% if the first seizure is at 1 year of age and about 30% at 2 years.
First aid: stay calm, lay the child on the side on a safe surface, put nothing in the mouth, time the seizure, and call for help or give rescue medicine if it lasts 5 minutes or more.
Routine immunisation should continue.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling a seizure as febrile without excluding meningitis, particularly in infants, children given antibiotics, or those not back to baseline.
Starting long-term antiepileptics, or aggressive antipyretics or tepid sponging, to prevent recurrence; neither works.
Missing mimics: rigors, febrile delirium, breath-holding spells, syncope and cardiac arrhythmia.

drugs.name: Midazolam (buccal or intranasal)
drugs.dose: 0.3 mg/kg once (max 10 mg); may repeat once after 5 to 10 minutes
drugs.notes: First line when there is no IV access; seizure lasting 5 minutes or more.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg); may repeat once after 5 to 10 minutes

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg IV (max 10 mg) or 0.5 mg/kg rectally (max 10 mg)

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 hours (max 60 mg/kg/day)
drugs.notes: For comfort only; does not prevent recurrence.
